Weakly-informative default priors for a failure-rate hazard model

Source: R/discrete-time-hazard-brms.R
build_hazard_prior.Rd

Supplies a sensible starting prior for the model build_hazard_spec assembles, keyed to each parameter's intercept and robust to whatever covariates the dpar_formulas add. For every parameter the chosen functions need, it sets a weakly-informative prior on the intercept (the parameter's value at the reference temperature and start of exposure), a generic Normal(0, 1) on any covariate slopes, and an Exponential(2) on the standard deviation of any random effect. The slope and random-effect priors are added only when the parameter actually has those terms, so brms raises no "no parameter" warning. Override the centre of any parameter through intercept_priors, or the shared slope and random-effect standard-deviation priors through slope_prior and sd_prior; or replace the whole set with your own prior when fitting with fit_hazard().

Usage

build_hazard_prior(
  m_form,
  baseline = "mem",
  dpar_formulas = list(),
  intercept_priors = list(),
  slope_prior = "normal(0, 1)",
  sd_prior = "exponential(2)",
  costressors = list(),
  long
)

Arguments

m_form

A character string denoting a key of M_catalogue (e.g. "exp" or "exp_threshold").

baseline

A character string denoting a key of h0_catalogue: "mem" (default), "weibull", "llogis" or "gompertz".

dpar_formulas

A named list of one-sided formulas, one per parameter, as in build_hazard_spec. A parameter's fixed and random terms decide which slope and standard-deviation priors are added.

intercept_priors

A named list of prior strings, one per parameter, that replace the default intercept (centre) for those parameters, e.g. list(Tc = "normal(26, 4)"). A parameter left out keeps its default; a name that is not a parameter of the chosen functions is ignored with a warning.

slope_prior

A single prior string for every covariate slope (a population-level effect beyond the intercept), applied to each parameter that has one. Defaults to "normal(0, 1)".

sd_prior

A single prior string for every random-effect standard deviation, applied to each parameter that has one. Defaults to "exponential(2)".

costressors

An optional list of costressor objects, as in build_hazard_spec. Each adds an intercept prior for its main effect and, when the temperature interaction is kept, its interaction coefficient. Defaults to none.

long

A data frame, the row-per-interval table from build_hazard_data that the prior is for. The defaults read from it the reference time tau_ref, the reference temperature Tr and the temperatures at which failures were observed. It has no default. fit_hazard() passes its own table when it builds the default prior.

Value

A brmsprior.

Details

The defaults take three things from the data in long, so that they say the same thing whatever the organism, the time unit and the length of the exposures: the reference time tau_ref, the reference temperature Tr, and the median temperature at which failures were observed, T_f. They are weakly-informative and meant to be changed to suit your study:

  • loga – log amplitude. Stated where the failures are: at T_f, the cumulative hazard reached over tau_ref is centred at exp(-1), about 0.37, with a standard deviation of 2 on the log scale (about 0.007 to 20). With the memoryless and Gompertz baselines a is a rate per unit time, so that centre is -1 - log(tau_ref); with the Weibull and log-logistic it is -1. The prior is then carried from T_f back to the temperature a refers to (see below).

  • logb ~ normal(-0.7, 1) – log temperature sensitivity

  • logc – log baseline term of the power function (see below)

  • Tc ~ normal(T_f, 3) – critical temperature, centred where failures were observed

  • logshape ~ normal(0, 1) – log Weibull / log-logistic shape

  • logscale ~ normal(log(tau_ref), 1) – log log-logistic scale

  • gam ~ normal(0, 3 / tau_ref) – Gompertz rate: the baseline hazard changes by a factor of exp(gamma tau_ref) across the reference time, within about 400-fold either way with 95% probability. It is centred at zero, the memoryless case, so unless the data show a trend the fit stays near a flat baseline.

with normal(0, 1) on any covariate slope and exponential(2) on any random-effect standard deviation. Each co-stressor in costressors adds a normal(0, 1) on its main effect c<name> and a tighter normal(0, 0.5) on its temperature interaction dT<name>, both overridable through intercept_priors.

The prior on a when the reference is far from the failures

For the rates anchored at the reference temperature (exp, zeroexp, zeropower, power), a is the rate at Tr, or its scale there, and Tr may lie a distance d = T_f - Tr from where failures were observed. The log rate at T_f is then loga plus a term in b and d (b d for exp), so loga is the log rate at T_f less that term, and it inherits the uncertainty in b across the distance:

  • its centre is the centre at T_f less the term at the prior median of b;

  • its variance is 2^2 plus the square of (the change in the term per unit of b, times the prior standard deviation of b).

For exp this is normal(centre - 0.5 d, sqrt(4 + (1.07 d)^2)): the usual prior when the reference is at the failures (d = 0), and a much wider one 14 degrees below them. A prior of standard deviation 2 on loga at a distant reference would in effect be a tight prior on b, and biases it. The threshold functions are anchored at Tc, not Tr, and take the centre at T_f unchanged. The calculation uses the default prior on logb; if you change that prior and keep a distant reference, set loga to match.

The baseline term c of the power function

In M(T) = c + a (T - Tr)^b, c is the rate that remains at the reference temperature: failure that happens whatever the warming. Its default is centred so that about 1% of individuals would fail over tau_ref for reasons unrelated to temperature, normal(log(0.01) - log(tau_ref), 2) with the memoryless or Gompertz baseline and normal(log(0.01), 2) otherwise, which covers background failure from about 0.02% to 40%. The 1% is a judgement, not a measured value. Where controls were held at the reference temperature, set it from them: if a fraction q of controls failed over a time t, c is about -log(1 - q) / t, so for instance intercept_priors = list(logc = "normal(log(-log(1 - 0.02) / 120), 1)") for 1 in 50 failing over 120 minutes.

Examples

# A ramp from 20 to 35 degrees over 60 minutes, with two failures.
path   <- ramp_path("A", T_start = 20, rate = 0.25, t_max = 60)
checks <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = seq(0, 60, by = 10))
ind    <- data.frame(id = 1:3, path_id = "A", event = c(1, 1, 0),
                     t_upper = c(30, 40, 60), acclim = c(10, 15, 15))
long   <- build_hazard_data(ind, path, "interval", covariates = "acclim",
                            checks = checks)
#> ℹ The intervals at risk were divided further, into 277 rows from 13, so that
#>   temperature changes by at most 0.1 degrees within each.
#> ℹ The hazard is taken as constant within an interval, which biases the fit when
#>   temperature changes much within it. Failures at a known time are also given a
#>   short closing interval, so their hazard is that of the moment of failure.
#> ℹ Set `grid_dT` to change the step, or to `Inf` to keep the intervals as given.
#> Warning: ! For 2 individuals, temperature changes by up to 2.5 degrees within the
#>   interval in which failure was found.
#> ℹ That interval cannot be divided, since where in it the individual failed is
#>   not known, and the hazard is taken at its midpoint, so the estimates may be
#>   somewhat biased.

# Default weakly-informative priors for an exponential-threshold + Weibull model.
build_hazard_prior("exp_threshold", baseline = "weibull", long = long)
#>            prior class      coef group resp dpar    nlpar   lb   ub tag source
#>    normal(-1, 2)     b Intercept                     loga <NA> <NA>       user
#>  normal(-0.7, 1)     b Intercept                     logb <NA> <NA>       user
#>  normal(27.5, 3)     b Intercept                       Tc <NA> <NA>       user
#>     normal(0, 1)     b Intercept                 logshape <NA> <NA>       user

# Override a couple of priors (a cooler species, a tighter amplitude) and narrow
# the covariate-slope prior; every other parameter keeps its default.
build_hazard_prior("exp_threshold", baseline = "weibull",
  dpar_formulas = list(loga = ~ 1 + acclim),
  intercept_priors = list(Tc = "normal(26, 4)", loga = "normal(-6, 1.5)"),
  slope_prior = "normal(0, 0.5)", long = long)
#>            prior class      coef group resp dpar    nlpar   lb   ub tag source
#>  normal(-6, 1.5)     b Intercept                     loga <NA> <NA>       user
#>   normal(0, 0.5)     b                               loga <NA> <NA>       user
#>  normal(-0.7, 1)     b Intercept                     logb <NA> <NA>       user
#>    normal(26, 4)     b Intercept                       Tc <NA> <NA>       user
#>     normal(0, 1)     b Intercept                 logshape <NA> <NA>       user
